name: Lena Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and this is confidential. What happens on an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a mountain line crew replacing bare wire with covered conductor to reduce fire risk. My two-year technical diploma helps with the plans, but I still check each slope and each harness before the truck goes up. I like seeing a safer line over a dry valley.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Marco and I run a small weekend training school for new climbers. Our grown children are away from home, and we have saved well from my higher crew pay. I use AI daily for weather and permits at work and for bookings at the school; the heat wears me out more than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the mountain crew that my AI weather and permit summary is still handy even if the big predictions fade. We still have slopes to climb and covered wire to fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, my husband, and I have more than six months saved and a steady little training school on weekends. My crew lead wage is high for the trade, and there are other utilities within reach, so our income feels safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading line upgrades and using my existing AI summaries each morning. I would order the second practice pole for the school from our business budget, but only after Marco and I confirm the spring classes have enough paid enrolments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A useful tool that admits its limits beats a wonderful claim that cannot be checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many enrolments make the pole worth buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough paid places to cover the pole and fittings without using our household reserve. Marco and I will check the class ledger before we order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the crew’s training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already make everyone rehearse a harness check on the ground before we go up a slope, and that stays.

say: I would keep using my **weather summary** while acknowledging the wider AI change is small.
I would tell the crew that **mountain upgrades** still require trained climbers and checked harnesses.
think: Our **strong savings**, high wage and paid weekend classes make this world secure.
I value a **limited honest tool** more than a grand claim without field evidence.
do: Keep leading **covered-wire upgrades** and using existing AI summaries.
Buy a second **school practice pole** only if paid spring enrolments cover its cost.
S0.quote: A useful tool that admits its limits beats a wonderful claim that cannot be checked.
fieldNote: Her daily AI use is **existing practice**, while the pole purchase is a conditional business investment.
Paid enrolments must fund equipment without touching the **household reserve**.

steps.text: Keep leading mountain line upgrades and using existing morning summaries
Buy a second school practice pole only if paid spring enrolments cover it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AI may book and buy faster, but a closed mountain road makes a perfect schedule useless. I would get our training school to teach dispatchers what a real access check looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My field wage is still likely to hold, though the office may shrink. The school could gain pupils as workers try to change trades. Unpaid interest is not revenue for our training school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI dispatch controls at work when the company offers access and test them against three blocked-road jobs. At the school, Marco and I would add one paid evening class on route safety only after ten people enrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the office staff and curious about new pupils. My own household pay feels solid, provided the school does not spend ahead of bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why three blocked roads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One error can be odd weather, but three show whether the tool reads real access notes. I will keep the dates and road names for the dispatcher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only six people enrol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We do not run the extra class. Marco and I will not pay an instructor for empty seats just because the idea sounds timely.

say: I would insist on **real access checks** before AI dispatch sends crews up mountain roads.
I would offer a **route-safety class** only after the school has ten paid pupils.
think: My **field wage** appears secure while the office may need fewer planners.
The school might gain **new pupils**, but unpaid interest is not revenue.
do: Learn new **AI dispatch controls** and test three blocked-road jobs when access is offered.
Add a paid **school evening class** only after ten pupils enrol.
feel: **Uneasy** for office workers, confident about our own pay.
S1.quote: Unpaid interest is not revenue for our training school.
fieldNote: She links new dispatch learning to **company access** and tests it against real roads.
The new class creates a second revenue stream only when **ten paid enrolments** justify its cost.

steps.text: Learn AI dispatch controls when offered and test three blocked-road jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2028 can assemble permits, but a person still fits covered wire on a steep slope. Around 2031 a capable robot may climb as well, and I want our crew running the first mountain trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to leave full-time climbing around sixty two if the school and our savings keep performing. That would be before the robot date, but a fast office change might slow the school’s paid bookings, so I cannot treat the plan as guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the mountain crew while it pays and ask the utility for a paid robot-controls trial. If it posts a funded instructor vacancy, I would apply and learn the new controls on paid time; otherwise I would keep the school at its present size until our bookings are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with room to choose. I am more worried about giving apprentices a real place to learn than about paying next month’s bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you fund your own controls course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could afford a course, but I would choose one only for a posted paid vacancy. A certificate for a role nobody needs would not help our training school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the mountain trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot moving while a climber is in its swing path. I would stop the test and write down the exact movement before the maker tried again.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** handles permits before 2031 robots reach steep hands-on line work.
I would seek a **paid mountain trial** with the crew able to stop unsafe movement.
think: I hope to leave full-time climbing before **2031**, but school bookings could change that plan.
Our **savings** protect the household while apprentices face a shorter training runway.
do: Keep **mountain crew shifts** while paid work continues.
Apply for a posted **paid instructor vacancy** and learn controls on paid time if funded.
feel: **Uneasy** about fast change, with enough household money to plan.
S2.quote: A certificate for a role nobody needs would not help our training school.
fieldNote: She requires a **posted funded role** before committing to new robot-control training.
Her expected retirement precedes robots only if **school revenue and savings** hold up.

steps.text: Keep leading mountain line shifts while paid work continues
Apply for a posted funded instructor role if the utility offers one
Learn robot controls on paid time only if the funded instructor role is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years lets us test a robot through dust and gusts before 2034. The apprenticeship still needs someone who can tell a trainee to put a foot back down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 might speed permits, which I already check. If the school keeps paying and my health holds, I expect to have left regular climbing before hands-on robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present crew this year and offer the school’s existing safety classes with Marco. I would add a robot hazard lesson only if the utility shares real trial results and pays us to prepare it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own wages. A five-year lead gives me time to finish the mountain upgrades before handing over the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What results would you need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need near misses, failed stops and slope conditions. A polished video cannot teach a trainee where to stand on a windy slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early because of 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Marco and I already have a rough date; we will keep it only if the school, savings and my health support it.

say: I would ask for **dust-and-gust trials** before 2034 robots work on mountain lines.
I would keep **apprentice footing** and human judgement in the practical course.
think: I expect to stop regular climbing before **2034** if school income and health hold.
The **2031 permit change** looks manageable because I already check machine summaries.
do: Keep the **mountain crew** and existing school classes this year.
Add a **robot hazard lesson** only if real utility results and paid preparation are offered.
feel: **Calm** about near-term wages, interested in teaching trial lessons properly.
S3.quote: A polished video cannot teach a trainee where to stand on a windy slope.
fieldNote: The proposed new lesson depends on **results and funding**.
She keeps the current crew and school work; retirement remains **conditional**, not brought forward by this card.

steps.text: Keep mountain crew shifts and existing paid safety classes this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices a decade can give them proper climbing time before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would still make them practise a stop call on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our health, savings and school income stay sound, I expect to be out of regular line work before 2036. The school could keep running with Marco, but I will not pretend it needs the same hours from me forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would lead the mountain crew during 2026 and keep the existing school classes. In the first year after 2036, if I have retired from the utility as planned, I would review school bookings with Marco and teach only the paid sessions we can staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the household. I want the trade to remain open to young people who learn with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop climbing earlier because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our rough date depends on the school’s paid enrolments, savings and health, not on a robot date ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is one stop call students should practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trainee sees a frayed strap and calls stop before the bucket rises. We repeat the stop call until every trainee knows they can halt the lift.

say: I would protect **hands-on apprenticeship** time before thinking AI and 2039 robots reshape line work.
I would practise a **stop call** with each school trainee.
think: I expect to leave the utility before **2036** if health, savings and school income hold.
The school can continue after that, but only at **paid staffing levels** we can manage.
do: Lead the **mountain crew** and existing school classes during 2026.
After 2036, teach only **paid school sessions** if retired from the utility as planned.
feel: **Calm** about household income, committed to practical entry routes for trainees.
S4.quote: We repeat the stop call until every trainee knows they can halt the lift.
fieldNote: She explicitly separates **2026 work** from conditional school work after retirement.
No early exit is claimed; the existing date depends on **enrolments and health** as well as savings.

steps.text: Lead mountain crew shifts and existing school classes during 2026
Teach only paid school sessions after 2036 if retired and staffing covers bookings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most for apprentices, because robots could reach mountain work in 2031 before they build real hours. A paid trial role, posted training jobs and clear stop rules would help us teach them safely; Marco and I can cover our household bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a training place leads to a paid job. A school cannot honestly sell a future that has no posted vacancy.

headlineQuote: A school cannot honestly sell a future that has no posted vacancy.
portrait: **Lena**, 58, leads mountain line upgrades with a technical diploma, higher pay, strong savings and plenty of nearby utility jobs.
She uses **AI daily** and runs a paid climbing school with Marco alongside her regular crew work.
Her traditional focus on **apprenticeships** combines with an early appetite for new controls when paid roles and field evidence exist.
The **2028 case** worries her for trainees; her own planned exit depends on school revenue, health and savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives apprentices little time to build real mountain line hours before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid trials**, posted training roles and clear stop rules would support safe teaching.
